title: Short side and long side
summary: When Philidor is no longer possible: rook behind the pawn, king to the short side and checks from the long side.
part.short.title: Rook behind, king to the short side
part.short.summary: When the third rank is no longer possible: the rook goes behind the pawn and the king steps to the short side.
part.lateral.title: Checks from the side
part.lateral.summary: A bishop's pawn, the long-side mistake, and the side checks that hold a pawn on the seventh.
part.distance.title: Distance and recap
part.distance.summary: Why the rook needs three files, the king move Carlsen missed, and Karstedt's rules.
step.intro: Here the Philidor defence has come too late. It is Black to move, the king enters on f3 and your rook can no longer reach the third rank in time. For more than a hundred years this was thought to be lost. It is not. In 1897 Max Karstedt showed the defence, and it has three parts: the rook behind the pawn, the king to the short side and the checks from the long side. One at a time.
step.behindPawn: The black king has entered on f3 and threatens to advance the pawn. Only one move holds: the rook behind the pawn. Then, when the black king comes to defend the pawn and threatens mate, your king leaves the queening square. To which side?
step.behindPawn.hint: Re8: with the rook behind it the pawn cannot advance. Then the king goes to f1.
step.behindPawn.done: The king stepped out to the side with fewer files. That is this lesson's rule, and the reason comes next.
step.sides: The pawn splits the board into two sides. To its right there are three files left: the short side. To its left, four: the long side. Your king goes to the short side and leaves the long side free for the rook. King on the short side, rook on the long side. If the king went to the long side it would stand in the way of its own rook's checks, and on the other side the rook would have no room.
step.dance: The black rook checks. The king steps one square away and returns in front of the pawn as soon as it can. Your rook stays where it is, behind the pawn.
step.dance.hint: Kg2 and, when the black king steps aside, Kf2. On the new check, Ke1; and if the black king returns, Kf1 again.
step.dance.done: Black makes no progress: the pawn cannot advance with your rook behind it, and the black king cannot drive yours away from the queening square.
step.fpawn: The same defence with a bishop's pawn. Here the short side is only two files, and the king goes to g1. First the rook, then the king.
step.fpawn.hint: Rf8, behind the pawn. After Kf3, Kg1; on the check, Kh2.
step.fpawn.done: King on the short side, and the rook has the whole long side for its checks.
step.blunder: And this is the mistake. The king went to e1, the long side. Black checks on a1, the king goes to d2, and the black rook settles on f1, protecting the pawn from behind. The black king advances, the pawn goes with it, and your rook has no way to check from the side: on the short side there is no distance, and on the long side your own king is in the way. Lost.
step.lateral: The last part: the side checks. This position is Tarrasch's, from 1906. The pawn is already on the seventh, the black king in front of it. It looks like the end, but your king is on the short side and the rook is far away on the long side. It checks from the side, and the black king has only two ways out: walk away from the pawn, and then the rook attacks it, or come towards the rook, which is too far away to be reached.
step.checks: Give the checks. Every move is the only one: a side check while the king is near the pawn, and the rook behind the pawn when it walks away.
step.checks.hint: Ra1+, Ra2+, Ra3+, Ra4+, Ra3+ again and, with the black king far away, Re3.
step.checks.done: The black king walked all the way to the b-file to escape the checks, and the pawn was left alone. A draw.
step.distance: All of this depends on distance. Here the rook is on the b-file, not the a-file: one file closer. The checks run out one move sooner, because the black rook steps in between and the black king gets too close. Lost. The rule is to have at least three files between the rook and the pawn. That is why the king goes to the short side: so that the rook has the whole long side.
step.carlsen: Even the best get this wrong. In 2006 Magnus Carlsen was defending this position, with colours reversed, against Aronian. He gave a rook check, the attacking king stepped in front of the pawn and the game was lost. There was one move only, and it was a king move: leave the second rank, so that the rook can check without the king being in the way.
step.king: Play what Carlsen did not: the king to g3. Then the king returns and surrounds the pawn.
step.king.hint: Kg3. Then Kg2, Kf3 and Kf2.
step.king.done: The king stands beside the pawn on the short side, guarding e1, and the rook guards the first rank. A draw.
step.recap: Karstedt's three rules. One: if the third rank is no longer available, the rook goes behind the pawn. Two: when the king has to leave, it goes to the short side. Three: the rook takes the long side, at least three files from the pawn, and checks from the side when the pawn advances. And no hurry with the checks: sometimes the move is a king move.
step.t_behind: The black king has reached f3, and your rook can no longer get to the third rank. You defend with White. What holds the pawn now?
step.t_behind.hint1: Look for a square from which the rook stops the pawn from advancing.
step.t_close: King on the short side and rook on the other side, as with the side checks. But the rook is one file closer to the pawn. Do the checks still save the game?
step.t_close.hint1: Follow the checks and see when the black king gets close to the rook or the black rook steps in between.
step.finish: Now against the machine: rook behind the pawn, king to the short side and, if the pawn advances, checks from the side.
ex.e08: White to move and draw. The king is already on the short side, but your rook is glued to the pawn, doing nothing. Find it a better square.
ex.e08.hint: The farthest square on the eighth rank. From there, a side check on the second.
ex.e08.solution: Ra8 and, after Re1, Ra2+. The rook needs distance: from the a-file it gives the side checks without the black king reaching it. Rb8 also draws, but the a-file is the farthest.
ex.e11: White to move and draw. This is the starting point of Max Karstedt's manoeuvre, from 1897. The black king threatens mate on the first rank, and the black rook is on h2, right on the short side. Where does your king go?
ex.e11.hint: The black rook on the short side doesn't change the rule. Think about who will need the long side in a moment.
ex.e11.solution: Kf1! The king goes to the short side, even with the black rook there. After Rh1+, Kg2 attacks the rook, and the long side stays free for your rook to give checks. Kd1 loses: the king would stand in its own rook's way. Berger, in 1890, thought this position was lost; Karstedt showed the draw.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. The black rook blocks the e-file, and the pawn has reached the third rank. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: While the pawn was far away, there was time. Not anymore: the rook has to go where side checks work.
ex.e12.solution: Ra8! The rook takes the a-file, and after Kd2 comes Ra2+, the first side check. Any other move loses. The tablebases show that with the pawn further back the rook could still wait before going to the flank; with the pawn here, it's now or never.
ex.e13: White to move and win. Now you attack. Tarrasch's position, 1906: the black king is on the short side, but the black rook is too close to the pawn. Escape the checks.
ex.e13.hint: There are only two files between the black rook and the pawn. Walk the king toward the rook without abandoning the pawn.
ex.e13.solution: Kc7, the only move. After Ra7+, Kc8 (Kc6, Kd6 and Kd8 also win); on Ra8+, Kb7 (or Kc7), and when the black rook goes behind the pawn, Rd8, Kc7 protects the pawn and it queens. The black rook needed three files of distance: with two, the white king reaches it and gets back to the pawn in time.
ex.e09: White to move and draw. The black king is in front of the pawn and its rook blocks the checks. Wait on the first rank and bring the king.
ex.e09.hint: The rook goes to a1 and stays on the first rank. The king closes in on the pawn via f3 and f2; when the pawn reaches e2, the rook blocks it on e1.
ex.e09.solution: Ra1, Kf3, Kf2, Re1 and, when the black king steps away, Ra1 again. From the first rank the rook controls the queening square and threatens checks again; exchanging rooks would lose.
ex.e10: White to move and draw. The black king slipped away to e2. Drive it out and switch the rook to the long side.
ex.e10.hint: A check on f2, and then the rook goes to the a-file. When the pawn advances, side checks.
ex.e10.solution: Rf2+, Ra2, Ra3+ and Ra2+. After the check the rook takes the a-file, the farthest one, and the side checks hold: if the black rook blocks them, the exchange leads to a drawn pawn ending.
key.behind: The attacking king is already through: the third rank does not work, and only Re8, behind the pawn, draws. From ProfAngel's Lichess study, with colours reversed.
key.tarrasch: Tarrasch's position (1906), from Wikipedia, with colours reversed: king on the short side, rook on the long side, side checks. A draw.
key.close: The same idea with the rook one file closer: it loses. Wikipedia gives it as Grigoriev's (1937). Three files of distance, at least.
key.carlsen: Aronian against Carlsen, 2006, with colours reversed: only Kg3 draws; the rook check lost the game.
history: Philidor, in 1777, analysed what happens when the rook leaves the third rank early and concluded that the defender loses. Dufresne in 1863 and Berger in 1890 repeated the analysis. In 1897 the German teacher Max Karstedt, composer of more than a hundred studies, published the correction: the ending is drawn if the king runs to the short side and the rook waits to give side checks from the greatest possible distance. Tarrasch dealt with the ending in an article of 1906, and the side-check positions in this lesson are his. The tablebases have proved Karstedt right in everything. In practice the defence remains difficult: in 2006 Magnus Carlsen lost a drawn position to Aronian because he gave a check when the right move was a king move.
practice: Against the machine: the black king is already in and Philidor is no longer possible. Rook behind the pawn, king to the short side and, if the pawn advances, side checks. The goal is to draw.
